blocks.title: Feedback mechanism
blocks.text: A feedback mechanism is a regulatory process in which the output of a system is used to control the activity of the system itself.

items: Negative feedback: the output reduces the activity of the system. It is the most common form of regulation, controlling body temperature, blood glucose and hormone secretion. If body temperature exceeds the 37 C set point, thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus signal the thermoregulatory centre, which signals the sweat glands; sweating lowers the temperature, and once it is back at the set point the receptors stop signalling.

Positive feedback: the output increases the activity of the system and strengthens the original stimulus. It is less common and occurs where rapid, large changes are needed, as in blood clotting and childbirth. Uterine contractions send impulses to the hypothalamus, the pituitary releases oxytocin, oxytocin causes stronger contractions, and the loop continues until the baby is born.

blocks.text: Unregulated positive feedback can cause disease: in severe infection or inflammation, immune cells release proteins called cytokines that further stimulate the immune response, and if this is not controlled it can cause excessive inflammation and tissue damage.

blocks.alt: Top: five boxes from a change, through receptors, the control centre and effectors, to the set point restored, with a red line feeding back to the start. Bottom left: a negative feedback loop for overheating, from body temperature above 37 C to sweating and back to 37 C. Bottom right: a positive feedback loop for childbirth, from uterine contraction through the hypothalamus and oxytocin to stronger contractions.
blocks.caption: Elements of homeostasis and the two kinds of feedback (original diagram after topic 13.1).
blocks.long_description: A change in the internal or external environment is detected by receptors, which inform a control centre such as the hypothalamus; the control centre signals effectors, muscles or glands, whose response brings the body back to its set point, and the result feeds back to the receptors. In negative feedback the result switches the signal off: when body temperature rises above 37 C, sweat glands produce sweat until the temperature falls back and the receptors stop signalling. In positive feedback the result strengthens the signal: during childbirth uterine contractions lead to oxytocin release, which causes stronger contractions, until the baby is born.
